title: Brazil’s split signal: weaker credit-sensitive demand and a higher inflation path leave the Selic at 13.75%
summary: Brazil’s monetary policy committee unanimously held the Selic at 13.75% on 4 November. The minutes released on 10 November explain why evidence that high borrowing costs were working did so little to reassure the seven voters about inflation. They saw activity slowing more sharply than at the September meeting, especially in cyclical sectors. At the same time, recent supply shocks had lifted the inflation forecast, underlying inflation was accelerating and longer-term expectations were moving further from target. The committee judged that dislodged expectations called for greater restraint sustained for longer than would otherwise have been appropriate. It offered no date or size for the next move.

The domestic evidence helps locate transmission. The second-quarter GDP release had already shown moderation. More timely trade surveys subsequently suggested a turning point concentrated in credit-sensitive segments. Rates on freely negotiated loans were high for households and businesses alike. The labour market adjusted more slowly. Unemployment remained historically low. Employment growth and nominal pay growth were easing at the margin, but real earnings still grew faster than labour productivity. The committee was interested in how employment conditions flowed through wages to individual sectors’ prices. One implication is that weaker durable-goods sales could coexist with sustained services price pressure for some time. A single activity indicator would miss that difference in timing.

Four supply developments mattered to the deliberation. Conflict in the Middle East raised oil costs. El Niño threatened agricultural productivity and electricity costs. The end of the six-days-on, one-day-off working pattern affected labour costs. Domestic political uncertainty contributed to currency depreciation. Copom distinguished the direct price effects from subsequent changes in other prices and expectations. A sharper slowdown, with projected GDP growth below potential growth, could limit propagation. That argument concerns the growth rate. The committee simultaneously listed a positive output gap as a risk to services disinflation. An economy growing more slowly than potential can still start the period with demand above its sustainable level.

The conditional reference case used the Selic trajectory from the Focus survey, an initial exchange rate of R$5.20 per US dollar followed by purchasing-power-parity evolution, approximately six months of oil futures followed by 2% annual growth, and a green electricity tariff flag in December 2026. Table 1 put four-quarter headline IPCA at 5.6% in 2026, 4.7% in 2027 and 3.5% in the second quarter of 2028, the relevant policy horizon. Free prices were projected at 5.5%, 4.8% and 3.4% respectively, and administered prices at 6.0%, 4.2% and 3.9%. The source gives no numeric previous forecast in this table. The separate Focus inflation expectations were 5.2% for 2026 and 4.8% for 2027. Using those survey responses as if they were the committee’s projections would obscure the difference between public beliefs and a model conditioned on the surveyed interest-rate path. The R$5.20 starting value was a rounded average over the ten business days ending in the week before the meeting (footnote 2). Comparing it with a single spot quote on decision day would mix two observation windows. Although the oil assumption eventually grows at 2% per year, the contemporaneous Brent futures curve implied a decline over the second half of the year (paragraph 11).

The committee distinguished the immediate demand effects of fiscal policy from its effects on the term premium and the neutral rate. In the near term, public stimulus could support consumption, partly offsetting monetary restraint. Longer term, perceptions about debt sustainability could raise the term premium. It also saw weaker fiscal discipline, fewer structural reforms and expanded directed credit as possible influences on the neutral real interest rate. An increase in a long nominal yield could therefore reflect risk compensation even if markets made little adjustment to their near-term Selic expectations. The minutes identify this possibility without measuring either curve component or claiming that such a move followed publication.

The distribution of risks remained tilted upward. Sticky services prices, a persistently weaker exchange rate, further stimulus and longer-lasting effects on expectations sat on one side. A larger domestic slowdown, weaker global activity and lower commodity prices sat on the other. In paragraphs 15–18 the committee distinguished a restrictive policy level from an automatic reaction to each imported price rise. Its willingness to act firmly was conditional on second-round effects. Evidence that expensive credit was slowing private demand supported maintaining restraint, while faster core inflation and less well-anchored expectations limited the case for loosening that restraint.

questions.question: Which prices would show the four supply disturbances spreading beyond their original categories?
questions.detail: Track exposed energy, food and labour-intensive items alongside less directly exposed services and long-horizon expectations. Compare movements over several releases, accounting for seasonality, indexation and prior trends. More synchronised increases outside initially affected categories would support the committee’s concern about second-round effects. Reversals confined to the initial sectors as demand softened would support the alternative interpretation. The November minutes identify plausible channels but do not estimate their elasticities.

questions.question: Is the credit-sensitive slowdown spreading far enough to relieve labour and services pressure?
questions.detail: Match lending rates and new non-earmarked credit by borrower type with sectoral retail volumes, employment, real earnings, productivity and services inflation. Differences in exposure to bank borrowing and lags between sales and hiring matter. If consumer durables slow first while real pay outpaces productivity, weak retail totals alone provide incomplete evidence about the output gap or the persistence of domestically generated inflation.

questions.question: How much of a curve change would be attributable to expected Selic versus term premium?
questions.detail: Separate near-dated contracts spanning the release from longer yields and examine concurrent fiscal, oil and exchange-rate news. Compare changes around the decision and the separately timed minutes and use survey vintages consistent with each event. This would help identify whether revised expected policy, changed risk compensation or new external information best explains an observed move, subject to the usual limits of event identification.
